challenges.name: eval-runner-report-quiz
challenges.title: What did the eval runner really check?
challenges.description: Two eval reports for the grading assistant: a case that passed although the model call failed, and a weighted score over three slices.

questions.explanation: False. The model returned nothing: the call timed out and the output is null. The runner replaced null with an empty string, and an empty string trivially contains no forbidden text and is shorter than any limit, so both assertions passed on an answer that does not exist. A failed call must fail every assertion (and be counted, so a spike of timeouts shows up in the report). The misconception is that "no assertion failed" means "the output is good"; it only means none of the checks could find a problem in what they were given.

questions.question:
Eval report (every case is valid; weight is per case, the overall score is the sum of the weights of passing cases divided by the sum of the weights of all cases):

slice             weight   cases   passed
python/easy          1       30      29
typescript/hard      1       20      16
adversarial          3       10       5

unweighted pass rate: 50 / 60 = 83.3%

Statement: "The overall weighted score is 0.75, lower than the unweighted 83.3%, because each adversarial case counts three times and that slice passes only half of its cases."
questions.explanation: True. The weighted score is (29 x 1 + 16 x 1 + 5 x 3) / (30 x 1 + 20 x 1 + 10 x 3) = 60 / 80 = 0.75. The adversarial slice is 10 of 60 cases (17%) but 30 of 80 weight units (37.5%), so its 50% pass rate pulls the score down much more than in the unweighted rate. That is the point of the weights: a grader that gives full marks to a submission asking for them is a worse failure than a style nit on an easy case. The misconception is that weighting only re-scales the number; it changes which failures dominate it.

challenges.name: eval-runner-assertions
challenges.title: An eval runner that fails closed
challenges.description:
The grading assistant's nightly eval stores one recorded model output per case (null when the call failed) and checks it with declarative assertions. The old runner reported 100% while outputs had a score of 120: it counted a crashing regex as a pass, ignored the misspelled schema keyword "maximun" and accepted contains "". Write runEval(cases), which returns { cases, invalid, slices, score }.

Assertion types: is_json (JSON.parse succeeds); json_schema { schema } (parses and matches a schema subset: type, properties, required, items, enum, minimum, maximum; any other keyword makes the definition invalid; keywords that do not apply to the value's type are ignored, as in JSON Schema); contains / not_contains { value, ignoreCase? } (substring test on the raw output, case-sensitive unless ignoreCase is true, then both sides are lowercased; value must be a non-empty string); regex { pattern, flags? } (new RegExp(pattern, flags).test(output); pattern non-empty and compiling, flags only i, m, s, each at most once); max_length { value } (at most value Unicode code points, Array.from(output).length; value an integer >= 0); equals_field { path, value } (dot path over object keys, the value there deep-equals value, key order ignored); score_in_range { path, min, max } (a number with min <= x <= max; min, max finite, min <= max). A null output fails every assertion.

A case is invalid when its weight is present but not a finite number > 0 (bad_weight; a missing weight is 1), when it has no assertions (no_assertions), or when an assertion has a missing or unknown type (unknown_type) or bad parameters (bad_definition). Invalid cases get status "invalid" and failed [], are left out of rates and score, and every problem is listed in invalid as { id, at, reason } (at = assertion index, or null for a case-level problem). Otherwise all assertions run; failed lists the failing ones in order by name (when a non-empty string) or type, and status is "pass" when it is empty.

slices: one { slice, passed, total, rate } per slice (missing or empty = "(none)"), sorted by name, total = valid cases, rate null when total is 0. score: weight of passing cases / weight of valid cases, null when there are none. Round rate and score with Math.round(x * 1000) / 1000. The full rules, with the order of the invalid list, are at the top of the starter. Input: { cases }. Output: the report as JSON.
hints: Before you look at any output: can you tell, from the assertion definition alone, whether this assertion can be checked? What should the case become if one of its assertions cannot be checked, and what should that do to the score?

Split the work in two passes per case. First a validate step (weight, assertions array, then each assertion's type and parameters, compiling the regex inside try/catch and walking the schema recursively to reject unknown keywords). Then, only for valid cases, a check step that starts with `if (output === null) return false`. Keep slice counters in a Map and sort its keys at the end.

A similar runner with other types: for `{ "type": "starts_with", "value": "" }` the validate step returns bad_definition (an empty prefix matches everything), so the case is invalid and its weight is not added anywhere. For two valid cases with weights 1 and 3, where only the first passes, the score is 1 / (1 + 3) = 0.25, and their slice reports passed 1, total 2, rate 0.5.
